conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because you weren't feeling well—can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve just been really tired. Started a few days ago. I had a runny nose and cough, thought it was from the AC at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had some cramps and threw up a couple times. One loose stool, but nothing bloody.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your insulin—have you been taking it regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I missed a couple doses. I was just so tired, I forgot. I usually take Lantus at night and Humalog as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also saw your blood sugar was very high—over 700—and your body’s in a state called diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That’s why you feel so unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… like last time? That was scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, similar. But we’re going to treat it right away. You’re getting fluids through your IV to rehydrate, and we’ve started an insulin drip to bring your sugar down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my potassium was high too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High blood sugar pulls fluid and electrolytes out of your cells, which affects potassium. But with fluids and insulin, it’s already starting to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My mouth’s been so dry, and I’ve been peeing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from the high sugar—your kidneys are trying to get rid of it. We’ll fix that. We also checked your kidney function, and it’s a bit impaired from dehydration, but it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been drinking beer—maybe three six-packs a week. Last one was two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That can definitely affect your diabetes control and contribute to DKA. But your alcohol level was zero now, and no signs of withdrawal, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to drink anymore. It’s just hard sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help with that. We’ve started you on thiamine and folate—important vitamins that can be low with alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to know. What about my cough and runny nose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray—it looks clear, no pneumonia. Your symptoms are likely from a mild cold or allergies. We can give you loratadine if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. My eyes are sensitive to light too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with DKA. It should get better as your sugars normalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your labs are improving—your acid levels are coming back to normal, and your potassium is now in a safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the insulin drip going to stay on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll transition you to your regular insulin tonight—Lantus at bedtime with Humalog as needed. The goal is to get off the drip by 9 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. I just don’t want to end up here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on that. Staying on your insulin, even when you’re not feeling well, is key. And cutting back on alcohol will help a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re off the insulin drip and doing well on your regular shots. Blood sugars are between 100 and 180.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I feel a little better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One thing—we checked your iron levels and found they’re low. You have iron deficiency anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. Any bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. We don’t know the cause yet, but we’re starting you on ferrous sulfate—a daily iron pill—to help build it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. Should I get tested more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your doctor will want to look into it further after discharge—maybe check your stomach or intestines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Less tired. I had a low sugar this morning though—felt shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we caught it—it was asymptomatic, but we gave you glucose paste. It’s common when adjusting insulin. We lowered your Lantus from 36 to 32 units to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I’ll take 32 at night now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And keep using Humalog with meals based on your sugar. We’ll make sure you have supplies when you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function has improved—creatinine is back to normal. That means the dehydration is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ll drink more water at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And keep monitoring your sugars. If you’re sick, don’t stop insulin—even if you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your blood cultures came back negative—no infection. That’s great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my cold wasn’t making me worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have contributed, but it’s not serious. The main issue was missing insulin and drinking alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your insulin as prescribed—32 units Lantus at night, Humalog as needed. Take the iron pill daily. Stop drinking alcohol. And follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to come back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. If you need support with alcohol or depression, let us know—we can connect you with resources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ve given you prescriptions for insulin, iron, and your blood pressure medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—monitor for dizziness, shortness of breath, or if your sugars go too low or high. Call your doctor or come back if that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll check my sugars four times a day like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re doing the right things. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because you were found unresponsive at home. Do you remember what happened before that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No… I don’t remember anything. Was I asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a very low blood sugar—down to 20. That can cause someone to pass out. EMS gave you glucagon and sugar, but you were still confused and had some jerking movements, so they brought you in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I guess I didn’t eat much the day before. I’ve been drinking a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, alcohol and insulin together can be dangerous, especially if you’re not eating. Your blood sugar dropped so low it affected your brain. You were intubated briefly for safety, but we removed the tube yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on a ventilator? That’s scary. Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better now. Your mental status has improved. We did a head CT and EEG—no stroke or seizures were found. The brain changes are likely from the low sugar episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had jerking movements, but the EEG didn’t show seizure activity. It was likely a ‘provoked seizure’—caused by the severe hypoglycemia. As long as your sugars stay stable, it shouldn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I need to be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also treating you for alcohol withdrawal. Even though you didn’t have shakes or hallucinations, we’re giving you phenobarbital and thiamine to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking for years… it helps me sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But alcohol is making your diabetes harder to manage and may be linked to your depression. A social worker will talk to you about support programs like AA and our outpatient addiction clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really down lately. I don’t want to keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to talk about. You’re on venlafaxine and mirtazapine—we’ll restart those. We recommend dual diagnosis therapy for both depression and alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your magnesium was low, which can worsen confusion and heart rhythm. We’re giving you supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from drinking too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic alcohol use depletes magnesium and other nutrients. That’s why we’re also giving you folic acid, multivitamins, and thiamine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it affected so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does. We also noticed you have iron deficiency anemia. Your levels were very low. Likely from heavy periods. We’ve started iron pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired all the time. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Iron helps carry oxygen. We recommend seeing a gynecologist to check if your periods are too heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing your insulin. Your old 75/25 twice-daily regimen isn’t safe with alcohol and irregular eating. We’re switching you to long-acting glargine at night and rapid-acting lispro with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the difference?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glargine gives a steady background level. Lispro you take only when you eat, based on your sugar and meal size. This reduces the risk of lows if you skip a meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been scared to eat sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A diabetes educator will teach you how to use the new insulin and monitor your sugars four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved. It was likely from the antibiotics we gave briefly for possible aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for C. diff—came back negative. So it’s not an infection. We’ve given docusate to help with constipation from iron, but stop it if diarrhea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function was a little off when you came in, but it’s improving. That’s common after severe hypoglycemia and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking water much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please stay hydrated. We’re also adjusting your blood pressure meds. You’re now on lisinopril 10 mg and metoprolol XL once daily for better adherence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to forget the twice-daily one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The XL version lasts 24 hours. Much easier. We’ll also check your electrolytes and blood count in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Mentally, you’re back to baseline. You can do days of the week backwards now—great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple days. A home health aide will visit to help with meds and check in on sobriety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The diabetes educator went over your new insulin. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if my sugar is high before a meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll use the sliding scale on your lispro pen. The chart tells you how much to take based on your reading. Always eat after taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I don’t eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then don’t take lispro. Only glargine at bedtime, no matter what. That’s the key to avoiding another low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. Take all your meds as prescribed, eat regular meals, and avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The social worker will call to set up your outpatient appointments. Stay in touch with your primary doctor and check your labs as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists taking care of you. You're in the ICU because your blood sugar was very high and you're in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. Do you understand what that means?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been through this before. I think I forgot my insulin last night because I was drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely part of it. You had a pint of alcohol yesterday and missed your glargine. Your glucose was 751, and your pH was low at 7.04, which confirms DKA. We’ve started an insulin drip and are giving you IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been tired and just not checking my sugars. I know I should, but it’s hard with everything going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We also noticed your potassium was high at 5.7, but that’s improving with treatment. Your kidney function is affected too—your creatinine is up to 1.5, but we think it’s from dehydration, not new kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My mom has kidney problems from diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, it’s acute and likely reversible. Your baseline creatinine is 0.6, and with fluids, it’s already coming down. We’ve held your lisinopril for now to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my insulin? I was on 17 units glargine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on the insulin drip until your acid levels stabilize. Then we’ll restart glargine, probably at a lower dose—maybe 15 units. The endocrine team will help adjust your sliding scale too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble sticking to my regimen. I’ve been depressed and drinking more since my cousin passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ve consulted Psychiatry. They want you in an outpatient program, but you refused inpatient. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want to be locked up. But I do want help. I keep messing up my health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with a partial program—SOAP at ___—and a community support group through Vinfen. You’ll start intake in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. I need to get better. My kids need me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by being open. We also checked for infection—your chest X-ray was clear, flu test negative, and blood cultures show no growth. So no pneumonia or sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high at 13.3, but that’s common in DKA and not always from infection. It’s already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this dry cough. Is that from the DKA too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could also be from allergies—your history mentions rhinitis. But the X-ray shows no infection, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been itchy down there. Vaginal itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection in your urine, and no discharge reported. It might be related to high sugar levels. Once your glucose is controlled, that should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Glucose is down to 176, bicarb up to 17, and anion gap is closing. We’re turning off the insulin drip soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something? I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a regular diet. You’ll need to check your blood sugar regularly and give your own insulin. We’ll help you with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping my iron pills too. My last one was weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ferritin is low at 12, confirming iron deficiency. You’re still menstruating, which likely contributes. We’ve restarted your ferrous sulfate. You’ll need to take it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It upsets my stomach sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it with food or switch to a lower dose if needed. We’ll check your levels as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.0 and glucose is stable. You’re moving to the regular floor today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Less tired. I’ve been checking my sugars like I should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. The Psychiatry team met with you yesterday. Are you planning to go to the SOAP program?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m going next week. I think I need the support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also sending you home with ketone test strips. Use them if your sugar is high, especially if you feel sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember using those before. I just forget when I’m not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The goal is to catch DKA early. We’ll go over your discharge meds tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are looking good. Glucose 162, bicarb 20, creatinine 0.6—back to baseline. WBC is low at 2.5, but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the low white count a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It can happen after DKA. We’ll monitor it, but you’re not showing signs of illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad my kidneys are okay. I worry about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So do we. Staying hydrated and managing your sugars is key. Your neuropathy and retinopathy also need regular follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been to my eye doctor in a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please schedule that. Same with your PCP. You need to keep all your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all stays stable. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on the same insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 15 units of glargine at bedtime and use lispro on a sliding scale for highs. We adjusted it to reduce DKA risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—mirtazapine, Effexor, aspirin, statin, and your nasal spray. We’re continuing iron, thiamine, and folate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to stay on them this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. The support program will help. And call your doctor if your sugars are high or you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day in the hospital. Your exam is normal—clear lungs, normal heart, no swelling. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up for success. Keep your appointments, take your meds, and reach out for help when you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re strong for facing this. Let’s get your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before discharge. You’ve done great. Any last concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. I’ve got my prescriptions and follow-up dates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: ketone strips if sugar is high, call your doctor if vomiting or sick, and go to the ER if you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re proud of you. You’ve turned a corner. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go home today. Your condition is stable—alert, eating well, and walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll start the program and see my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. We’ll send all your records to your PCP. Call us if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU now. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really sick—nauseous, throwing up, and my blood sugar was through the roof. I had this abscess on my belly, and after a hot shower it started draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You also had very high glucose—731—and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s bad, right? I skipped my Lantus last night because I felt so off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That likely contributed. The infection on your abdomen also stressed your body. We drained the abscess in the ER, and you’re on antibiotics now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that serious. I just thought it was a pimple.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with insulin injections if the site isn’t clean. We’ll talk more about safe injection practices later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach still feels weird, but I’m not vomiting anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs show your kidneys were stressed—creatinine was 1.4—but that’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s likely from dehydration due to DKA. It should return to normal, which it’s already starting to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. My sugars have been so hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your insulin drip closely. Once your acid levels normalize, we’ll switch you to injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the same needle a few times… is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that increases infection risk. We’ll have the diabetes educator show you safer techniques.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work is improving. Anion gap is closing, and your pH is rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll transition you off the insulin drip today and restart your glargine at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 15 units. Should I go back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll monitor your sugars and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My belly incision is still draining a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The wound care team checked it—drainage is good, no need for more surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said something about a culture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they found Group B Strep and some Candida in the wound. That’s why you’re on vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not uncommon in skin infections. We’re treating it, and you’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been trying to eat, but not much stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on light foods. Small, frequent meals might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look great. Glucose is 120, bicarbonate is 18, and anion gap is nearly closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Getting there. We’ll keep you on IV antibiotics a bit longer, then switch to oral Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably a couple more days. We want to make sure your sugars stay stable and the wound keeps improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The diabetes nurse came by yesterday. I learned a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. She said you taught back the technique perfectly—clean swabs, rotating sites, new needles each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize how much I was cutting corners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens. The key is consistency. We also restarted your lisinopril—kidney function is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about my blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. We’ll keep monitoring. Your hemoglobin dropped a bit, but it’s likely from the infection, not bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your ultrasound shows no new fluid pockets. The area is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The drainage is sufficient. We’ll send you home with a nurse to help with dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Bactrim for five days. And we’re adjusting your insulin—12 units at breakfast and 12 at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To better match your body’s needs. We’ll fine-tune it at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll stick to it this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Your mental health and alcohol use are also important—we can connect you with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking less. Maybe I should talk to someone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. For now, focus on healing. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are normal. You’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue all your meds, especially insulin. Use new needles, clean sites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the visiting nurse will come?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily for dressing changes. Call us if the wound gets red, swollen, or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary doctor in a week and the diabetes clinic soon after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You’re here because of vomiting, high blood sugar, and feeling very weak. We’ve started you on fluids and insulin through your IV. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better since the fluids, but I was so sick earlier. My mouth was so dry, and I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was extremely high—over 1000. That’s what caused the diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. We’re treating it with insulin and fluids. We also placed a central line in your neck because your veins were hard to access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that thing in my neck? I felt them working on me but I was so out of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the central line. It helps us give you medications and fluids more easily. Your labs also showed very high potassium, which can be dangerous for the heart. We’ve treated that, and your EKG is looking better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? But I thought I was low on everything. I haven’t been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Even though your blood showed high potassium, your body is actually depleted overall. As we correct the DKA, the potassium will shift, so we’re watching it closely and replacing it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I skipped my Lantus for a couple days because I was nauseous and didn’t feel like eating. I thought maybe I didn’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely what triggered the DKA. Even when you’re not eating, your body still needs background insulin. Skipping it, especially with type 1 diabetes, can lead to this. We’ll help you adjust your doses before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. I’ve been trying. I haven’t had alcohol for a month now. I’m really trying to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ve started you on vitamins, including thiamine, just to support you. We’re also monitoring for any signs of withdrawal, but so far you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my kidneys—are they okay? Last time I was here, they were affected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was elevated to 1.9, but your baseline is around 0.6. This is due to severe dehydration from DKA. With fluids, it’s already improving. We expect it to return to normal, just like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my old abscess site—is it infected again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the site is healed and there’s no sign of infection. We checked your urine, blood, and chest X-ray—all clear. No source of infection this time. This DKA seems related to missed insulin, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee again. Your labs from this morning show improvement. Your blood sugar is down to 250, and your anion gap is closing. We’re transitioning you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean I can eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a light diet. But we know you have gastroparesis, so we’ll go slow. Small, frequent meals. The nurse will help you time your insulin with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate that my stomach empties so slowly. Makes it hard to manage insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with the diabetes educator to help you adjust. Also, your white blood cell count was high when you came in—15.1—but that’s common in DKA as a stress response. It’s already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I heard my count dropped later? I overheard a nurse say I was neutropenic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your WBC dropped to 2.9 yesterday evening, with low neutrophils. We don’t know why, but this pattern happened last time too. No fever or infection, so we’re watching it. It’s likely related to your diabetes fluctuations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, you’re not at risk because you have no fever or infection. We put you on neutropenic precautions—meaning we’re extra careful with hygiene. Your count is expected to rebound, as it did last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I’ll need to follow up on that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend an outpatient evaluation to understand why this keeps happening. But for now, your main issue was DKA, and you’re recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your kidney function has normalized—creatinine is 0.7. Potassium is stable at 4.1. You’re off the insulin drip and doing well on injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’ve been checking my sugars every few hours like they taught me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. But we noticed a few lows—like 60 this morning. That’s why we’re reducing your Lantus dose from 12 units to 10 in the morning and 5 at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize I was that low. I just felt shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hypoglycemia can be dangerous. We want to avoid that. The diabetes educator will review your sliding scale and meal timing before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll pay more attention. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is now 2.9, but neutrophils are up to 35%. You’re no longer neutropenic. It’s improving, just like we expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s rebounding? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It’s a strange pattern, but consistent with your history. Still, we recommend seeing a specialist to look into it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment. I’ve got my primary care next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your blood sugar is stable, kidneys are normal, and your CBC is improving. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about support at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll have a visiting nurse coming daily to help with glucose checks, insulin, and making sure you’re taking all your meds. We’re also assigning a case manager through your insurance to help coordinate services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I live alone, so it helps to know someone’s checking in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’re at high risk for readmission, so we want to give you every support. Keep your follow-up with endocrinology and your PCP. And please call if your sugars are high or low for more than a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no alcohol—I’m sticking to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll keep you on your depression meds—mirtazapine and Effexor. How’s your mood been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’ve been talking to my mom more. She’s proud I’ve been sober.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Support from family makes a big difference. We’ll see you one last time tomorrow before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final labs are excellent—normal kidney function, stable CBC, blood sugar 143. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Remember: take your insulin even when you’re not feeling well, watch for lows, and keep your appointments. The nurse will be by this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything’s wrong. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing your case. You were brought in this morning because of very high blood sugar and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but I was so sick yesterday—thirsty, nauseous, and my stomach hurt. I didn’t think it was this bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs showed a very low blood pH—6.95—which means your body was very acidic. That’s from not having enough insulin. Your glucose was 870, which is dangerously high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had DKA before. I try to take my insulin, but sometimes I get confused with the dial. My vision’s been blurry in my right eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely make it hard. We know you have diabetic retinopathy, so your vision issues may be related. We’ll make sure your insulin doses are clear and simple.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I don’t want to keep coming back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to help you avoid that. Right now, you’re on an insulin drip to slowly correct the acid levels. We also saw your potassium was very high—7.3—when you arrived.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? But I thought diabetes made things low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. In DKA, potassium can shift out of cells, making it high in the blood—even if your total body potassium is low. We gave you treatment in the ER to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the EKG showed something. Was my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had peaked T waves, which can happen with high potassium. But after treatment, your EKG improved. No damage to your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started you on IV fluids to rehydrate you. Your kidneys were stressed—creatinine was 1.4—but that’s expected in DKA and should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much. I’ve been nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now and transition to oral intake as you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs are improving. Your pH is up to 7.25, and glucose is coming down. We’re going to keep the insulin drip a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my potassium? Is it still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it dropped quickly after treatment. We had to give you potassium through the IV because your total body stores are low. It’s a tricky balance in DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I needed it even though it was high at first?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Once insulin starts working, potassium goes back into cells, and levels can crash. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had no idea it worked like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people don’t. We’ll go over this more before you leave so you can recognize warning signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your acid levels have normalized. We’re going to stop the insulin drip and switch you back to your long-acting insulin—Lantus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 10 units in the morning and 7 at night. Is that what I’ll go back to?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting it. You’ll now take 10 units twice daily—morning and night. We’re increasing the nighttime dose to help control your morning sugars better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll still use the sliding scale for high readings. But we want to avoid low sugars, so we’re making the doses more consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had lows before. They scare me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. That’s why we’re adjusting carefully and will set up follow-up with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your blood count. Your white blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets are all a bit low—what we call pancytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: More likely related to your history of alcohol use. It’s often reversible with abstinence and good nutrition. We’re giving you thiamine, folate, and multivitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve cut back, but I admit I still drink some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not judging. But reducing further will help your blood counts, liver, and overall health. Social work can help connect you with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. I don’t want to keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look much better. Creatinine is down to 1.1, potassium is stable, and your CBC is slowly improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my vision? Will that get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blurriness may improve with better sugar control. But you should see an eye doctor soon to check your retinopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been in a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule a referral before you leave. Same for your foot numbness—we know you have diabetic neuropathy, so podiatry follow-up is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your insulin exactly as prescribed—10 units morning and night. Check your sugars four times a day. Use the sliding scale if they’re high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check for ketones in your urine. If they’re moderate or high, or if you’re vomiting and can’t keep fluids down, come in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual medications—mirtazapine, Effexor, lisinopril, atorvastatin. We’re sending a list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate you explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your labs are stable, and you’re feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments: endocrinology in one week, primary care in two weeks, eye doctor and podiatry soon after. Social work will call to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come to the ER if it’s urgent. Don’t wait if you’re not feeling right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care of yourself, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad I’m going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’ll be following up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember—insulin, check sugars, and call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Insulin, sugars, call if sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because your blood sugar was very high and you had been drinking. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I had a rough day yesterday. I was feeling really down, so I drank a whole bottle of vodka. I forgot to take my insulin that night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when did you realize your blood sugar was high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My visiting nurse came by this morning and said it was 'high'—she couldn’t even get a number. I gave myself 10 units of Lantus and 8 of Humalog, but it was still over 400 in the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your blood sugar was 479 when you arrived, and your body was in a state called diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That means your body started breaking down fat for energy because it didn’t have enough insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been here before for that. It’s scary. But I didn’t feel that bad this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes DKA can develop without severe symptoms at first. We’ve started you on an insulin drip and IV fluids to correct it. Your labs also showed your blood was acidic, but we’re fixing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel kind of tired? I didn’t throw up or anything this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fatigue is common. We’re monitoring you closely. Your breathing and heart are stable, and your chest X-ray showed no infection, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing a little since this morning. Is that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cough isn’t related to DKA. Your lungs are clear on exam and the X-ray didn’t show pneumonia. It could be mild irritation or something minor. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I haven’t eaten since yesterday morning, though. Could that be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could contribute to how you’re feeling. We’re giving you fluids with electrolytes. Once your blood sugar stabilizes, we’ll get you something light to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you—your latest blood test shows your acid levels are improving. Your anion gap is coming down, which means the DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But earlier my blood sugar dropped to 63. I got shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You got D50 and orange juice, and it came back up. That’s why we adjusted your IV fluids. We’re being careful not to drop it too fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to keep doing this. I know the drinking makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. Alcohol can interfere with your diabetes control and increase your risk of DKA. The social work team and BEST team are here to help. They can connect you with a rehab program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I want that. I’ve been trying to stop, but I keep falling back when I feel depressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very common. We’re continuing your Effexor and mirtazepine for depression. The BEST team will meet with you tomorrow to set up an outpatient intake appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had some crackers and juice. My blood sugar was 150 an hour ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re transitioning you off the insulin drip and back to your regular insulin shots—10 units of Lantus in the morning and at bedtime, plus sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble reading the insulin pen lately. My vision’s not great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your retinopathy makes it harder. We’ll go over insulin techniques again before you leave. Maybe a nurse can help you practice with a trainer pen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look much better. Your glucose is 166, potassium is normal, and your acid-base balance has corrected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the DKA is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your anion gap is now 11, which is normal. That means your body has stopped producing ketones. You’re responding well to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? Last time I was here, they said I was anemic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is still low at 9.1, but stable. It’s likely related to your history of alcohol use and chronic illness. We’re continuing your iron and folic acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure’s a little high today—158 over 89.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. We’re keeping you on metoprolol. We held your lisinopril temporarily to avoid potassium issues, but you’ll restart it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The BEST team met with you earlier. How did that go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was helpful. They’re setting me up with an outpatient program next week. I’m nervous, but I want to do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big step. They’ll support you with counseling and medical supervision. It’s great you’re taking charge of your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your condition is stable, and you’re back on your regular insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar regularly. If it’s over 250 for two checks in a row, test for ketones. Drink fluids, eat regularly, and don’t skip insulin—even if you’re not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling depressed again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your Effexor and mirtazapine. Call your psychiatrist or go to the ER if you have thoughts of harming yourself. And keep that appointment with the alcohol program—it’s a key part of staying healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re doing the right thing. Your family will be contacted, and you’ll follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re alert, breathing well, and your vitals are stable. All set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. I’ll take this one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best way. You’re going home with your usual medications, including insulin, blood pressure pills, and antidepressants. The discharge instructions have all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have the rehab appointment. I’m going to stick with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful to hear. We’re proud of you. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m going to call my mom when I get there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because your blood sugar was extremely high when EMS brought you in. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was feeling sick, throwing up. I couldn’t keep anything down, so I didn’t take my insulin. I also had some vodka the night before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When you’re vomiting and miss insulin, your body can go into diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. Your blood sugar was over 1100, and your pH was very low—6.91—which is dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t realize it was that bad. I just felt cold and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were also very dehydrated and had a low blood pressure—66 over 35 at one point. We gave you fluids and started an insulin drip to bring things under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the IV. Was I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, DKA can be life-threatening. But we caught it early and started treatment right away. You’re responding well. We also gave you sodium bicarbonate because your blood was too acidic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s good. What about my heart? I saw wires when I woke up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ECG. You had some changes—peaked T waves and ST depressions—which can happen with high potassium or acidosis. But your troponins were normal, so no heart attack. It’s likely due to the DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high potassium before. Was it bad this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 7.4, which is very high. We treated it with insulin and calcium to protect your heart. As your blood sugar comes down, your potassium is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? Last time I was here, my creatinine went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was elevated to 1.7, but that’s due to dehydration from high glucose. We call it pre-renal azotemia. With fluids, it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been trying to manage my diabetes better, but when I get sick, it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Illness and vomiting make it tough. But missing insulin, especially with alcohol, increases your risk of DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I’ve been working on my drinking. I went to a few outpatient sessions after last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll make sure you’re connected with support again before discharge. Your mental health and substance use are just as important as your diabetes.
