conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ve started you on thiamine and vitamins to help with that. We’re also watching for withdrawal, but your score is low so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood gas shows your pH is now 7.11. That’s a big improvement from 6.85. Your body is starting to balance out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re slowing the insulin drip and will switch you to injections once your levels stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pH is now 7.27, and your glucose is down to 180. We’re turning off the insulin drip soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on light food. We’re also restarting your lisinopril for blood pressure, but we’ll watch your numbers closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your troponin, which is a heart enzyme. It’s elevated, but you didn’t have chest pain, and your EKG and echo were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I had a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely ‘demand ischemia’—your heart was under severe stress from DKA, which can cause temporary injury. We don’t think you had a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on aspirin and statin, and recommend a stress test after discharge to check your heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count was high at first—14.8—but it’s likely from the DKA, not infection. We stopped antibiotics since there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I hate being on so many meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function was impaired—creatinine was 2.0—but that’s improved to 1.1 now. Likely due to dehydration and low BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys were always a little off. Last time they bounced back too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this looks like pre-renal injury from the DKA. With fluids and treatment, they’re recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your glucose is stable at 120, pH is normal, and creatinine is down to 0.9.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’re increasing your long-acting insulin to 16 units twice daily, up from 15 in the morning and 5 at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the increase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your body needs more insulin to stay stable, especially with your history of missed doses and alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to do better. I’m in an outpatient program for drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’re discharging you with thiamine and continuing your other vitamins and iron.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat troponin is trending down—from 0.28 to 0.21—supporting that the heart stress is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my echo showed nothing wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart muscle is thickened from long-term high blood pressure, but it’s pumping normally. The main issue was the temporary stress from DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is running high—around 150 over 90. We’ve restarted your lisinopril, but you may need a dose increase later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stress makes it worse. I’ll check it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs show your glucose is 95, sodium is normal, and white count is down to 3.3—perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney function back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is 0.7—back to your baseline. Great improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll follow up with your endocrinologist in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heart test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, schedule a stress test with your cardiologist. It’s precautionary, not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. All your labs are stable. You’re alert, breathing well, and your glucose is 88 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being discharged home with services. Continue all your meds, especially the new insulin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep up with your alcohol treatment and follow-up appointments. Call us if your blood sugar goes above 300 or below 70.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to be back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care of yourself. You’re strong—you’ve turned this around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—your mental status is clear, you’re walking independently, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. Home health will visit to check your insulin and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I live alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll help ensure you’re adjusting well. Call your doctor if anything feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your daughter is here. We reviewed your discharge plan with her too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s been so supportive. I’m lucky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Family support makes a big difference. Keep communicating with her and your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the ICU because your blood sugar was extremely high and you're in diabetic ketoacidosis. Do you know what that means?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been here before. It’s when my body starts breaking down fat because it doesn’t have enough insulin, right? I feel like I did last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your blood sugar was over 1100, your pH was very low, and you had high ketones. We’ve started you on an insulin drip and fluids. Do you know why this might have happened this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My glucose meter broke, so I couldn’t check my sugars. I was still taking my long-acting insulin, but I only took 4 units of Humalog with meals instead of adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Not adjusting your fast-acting insulin during illness can lead to DKA. You also had nausea and vomiting—did you think it was a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt sick for a few days. Stomach pain, throwing up. I thought it would pass, but it just got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs and urine—no signs of infection. So it’s likely a viral illness combined with not taking enough insulin. We’re giving you IV fluids and potassium, and we’ll keep the insulin drip going until your levels stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My chest felt tight earlier—was that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your EKG showed some ST depressions, and your troponin is slightly elevated. But since you don’t have blockages, we think it’s ‘demand ischemia’—your heart was under stress from the high sugars and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a typical one. It’s more like your heart was working too hard. As your DKA improves, the strain should go down. We’ll keep monitoring your EKGs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. My kidneys—are they okay? Last time I had issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was high at 2.4, but that’s likely from dehydration. We’ve stopped your lisinopril for now, and your levels are improving. We’ll restart it once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been taking my blood pressure pills regularly either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you get back on track. We’re also watching your potassium—it was very high earlier, so we gave you calcium gluconate to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that shot. It made my face feel warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Your levels are coming down. We’ll keep adjusting your insulin and fluids overnight. Try to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down, and your acid levels are improving. The insulin drip is helping. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Nausea’s gone. Can I have some ice chips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can have ice chips. We’re still holding food until your levels stabilize more. We’re also watching your white blood cell count—it was high but seems to be from the DKA, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking—just trying to stay in my outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. We’re giving you thiamine and vitamins just in case. Social work will help you reconnect with your program after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood gas shows your pH is improving—up to 7.33. That’s a big step. We’re going to try switching you to subcutaneous insulin soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more IV insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try, but sometimes the acid levels can rebound. If that happens, we might need to go back on the drip for a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll make sure to check my sugars more often when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to subcutaneous insulin, but your anion gap reopened. So we’ve restarted the insulin drip for now. It’s not uncommon—your body just needs more time to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was doing so well. Is something wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is part of the process. Your metabolism is still adjusting. We’ll keep the drip a little longer and try again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your bicarb is up to 18 and your gap is closed. We’re switching you back to subcutaneous insulin. You’re also having some hypoglycemia, so we’re giving you IV dextrose until you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky sometimes. Is that from low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a sign. We’re monitoring closely. Once you can keep food down, we’ll stop the IV sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin peaked at 0.28 but is now coming down. EKGs are improving too. This supports that it was demand ischemia, not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need a stent or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll continue aspirin and high-dose statin. You should follow up with cardiology for a stress test later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 0.7—better than your baseline. We’ve restarted lisinopril. Your blood pressure is a bit high, so we’re adding amlodipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I need to take my pills more regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re giving you a new glucose meter and strips so you can check your sugars. A diabetes educator will go over how to adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dropped to 2.9—mild leukopenia. It’s likely from the viral illness and your history. We’ll check it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s expected after DKA. Just avoid sick people and wash your hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Off IV fluids, eating normally, and your labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my insulin? It’s different now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on 15 units of glargine twice daily—down from 18—and continue the sliding scale. The educator will review it with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril and amlodipine. We’ll adjust doses based on your readings. Check them daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. You’re on aspirin now too, for heart protection. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to see a dentist? My teeth hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted poor dentition. Please schedule a dental check-up. Other than that, follow up with your primary doctor, endocrinology, and cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay on your insulin, check your sugars, and call if you’re sick or can’t keep food down. You’re going home with services to help with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Your vitals are stable, labs are good. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. I won’t let this happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Keep in touch with your care team. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m just signing your discharge papers. You officially discharged as of now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll head home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Remember to follow up in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick call to confirm—yes, your discharge is complete as of 8:05 AM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the ICU. You were brought in because you were confused and not making sense to your family. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I... I don’t really remember. I was sick, throwing up dark stuff. My son called someone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your son called 911. You were in diabetic ketoacidosis—your blood sugar was extremely high, over 1200, and your body was very acidic. We’ve started treatment with IV fluids and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no... again? I know I haven’t been checking my sugar. My meter broke, and I didn’t get a new one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s part of it. Your potassium was dangerously high too, and your kidneys weren’t working well. We gave you medicine to protect your heart and help lower the potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so weak. Did I need a breathing tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When you came in, you were breathing fast but starting to tire. Your blood gases showed worsening acidosis and rising CO2, so we had to intubate to support your breathing. You’re on a ventilator now but doing much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared. Is my heart okay? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned you had a mild heart attack—what we call an NSTEMI. It’s likely due to the stress of DKA and your underlying heart disease. Your troponin went up a bit, but your echo showed your heart is pumping strongly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no damage? I’ve had two heart attacks before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The damage appears small. Your heart function is actually hyperdynamic—pumping harder than normal. But because of your history of not taking medications consistently, cardiology decided medications are safer than procedures right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I mess up. I stop taking things when I feel bad or can’t afford them. And I’ve been drinking less, but it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why we’ve involved psychiatry. They think starting a new antidepressant—Zoloft—will help, and they recommend a partial hospitalization program for depression and alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried that before. I didn’t stick with it. But maybe this time...

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you. You’ve already agreed to the program, and your family is involved. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs are improving. Your acid levels are correcting, and your potassium is down to 5.1. We’ve turned off the insulin drip and started you back on long-acting insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re removing the breathing tube soon. Once you’re breathing on your own and tolerating food, we’ll move you out of the ICU. Your kidney function is also improving—creatinine is down to 1.8 from 2.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they put a dialysis line in. Did I need dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We used it for ultrafiltration to help your kidneys rest. But you responded well to fluids and insulin, so no ongoing dialysis is needed. Your urine output has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re off the ventilator now and doing well. We’re transferring you to the medical floor tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel more like myself. But I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body went through a lot. Your white count was high at first but is now coming down. We’re confident there’s no infection—your cultures were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is still a bit high—around 350—but much better. We’ve started a sliding scale with fast-acting insulin before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to get back to checking it myself. Can I use my old meter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with a new FreeStyle Lite meter and strips. You’ll check four times a day. Also, we’re adjusting your insulin: 16 units of glargine at breakfast, 2 at bedtime, plus sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to start an insulin pump last time. I never did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed that. Given your current stability and the need to rebuild routine, we think injections are safer for now. We can revisit the pump later with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are excellent. Glucose is 180, potassium 4.3, bicarbonate 24. Your kidney function has normalized—creatinine is 0.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on metoprolol, aspirin, and atorvastatin—important for heart protection. We restarted your lisinopril and amlodipine for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take Effexor and mirtazapine. What happened to those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry recommended switching to Zoloft. Mirtazapine can increase appetite and weight, which is harder with diabetes. Effexor was tapered off. You’ll take Zoloft daily now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. Walking, eating, managing your insulin. We’re planning for discharge in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about going home. What if I fall back into old habits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why the partial program is key. It’s daily therapy for both depression and alcohol use. You start in two days. Your daughter will help you get there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable, slightly low at 7.7. We think it’s from long-term alcohol use. You’re on folic acid and iron, which should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in over a week. I want to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge accomplishment. The program will support your sobriety. And your white count is low but stable—likely just a variant. We’ll check it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re focusing on discharge prep. You’ll go home with visiting nurse services to check on you daily for the first week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I live alone, but my daughter’s close.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: She’s listed as your emergency contact. You have follow-up with primary care, endocrinology, cardiology, and the addiction service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last labs look great. Glucose 150, creatinine 0.6, potassium 4.2. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it. I was so sick just days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up the insulin checks, take all your meds, and go to every appointment. The program is your best chance to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged today. Here’s your medication list and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll start the partial program Monday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. If you feel worse—shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion—go to the ER. Otherwise, see your PCP in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to get this right this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you can. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee. Just checking in. How are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but okay. I’m checking my sugar like I should. It’s been between 140 and 200.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good control. Any nausea or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just a little sore from the IV lines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That should fade. Keep up the good work. See you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your visiting nurse reported you’re doing well—eating, walking, taking meds. That’s great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. The Zoloft makes me a little nauseous in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try taking it with breakfast. If it continues, call your psychiatrist. Otherwise, keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One day until your program starts. Any concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nervous. But I know I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’re not alone. We’re all rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m calling to wish you well on your first day of the program. You’ve come so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m heading out now. I’m going to do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you will. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the ICU. You came in with very high blood sugar and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I was so sick this morning—nauseous, tired. My kids made me come. But I didn’t miss my insulin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you took your insulin. But your glucose was over 800, and your body was in serious acidosis. We’ve started fluids and an insulin drip to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Over 800? I thought it was just high. I didn’t know it could get this bad again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, especially with your history. You’ve had DKA before, and your kidneys were stressed too—your creatinine was elevated. But it’s likely from dehydration, not permanent damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My kidneys again? Last time I was here, they said I needed dialysis. Am I going to need that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not this time. Your kidneys are responding to fluids. We’re watching closely, but we don’t expect you’ll need dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about my heart? Last time I was here, I had a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked. Your troponin was slightly elevated, and there were some changes on the ECG, but you didn’t have chest pain. It’s likely stress on the heart from the DKA, not a new blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not another heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not an acute one. We’ll keep you on your heart meds—aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol—to protect you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been trying to stay on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Glucose is down to 150, and your acid levels are correcting. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still a little queasy, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched from IV insulin to a sliding scale. Soon we’ll restart your long-acting insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on that. Psychiatry and diabetes education are involved. They’ll help you build a safer routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been to the outpatient program, but it’s hard to keep up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re recommending more support—twice-daily home visits and family involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back. One showed a common skin bacteria, but only in one bottle. We think it’s contamination, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We stopped the antibiotics. Your white count is also coming down—it was likely a stress response from DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried about being on more meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is improving. Creatinine is down to 0.9. We’re almost back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my anemia? I always feel tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is still low, about 8.8. It’s likely a mix of nutritional issues. We’re continuing your iron, folate, and thiamine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take those every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That helps. We also had occupational therapy assess you. They’re concerned about memory and daily functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forget things. My daughter helps me with shots sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry thinks long-term diabetes and past alcohol use may have affected your cognition. But you’re not a danger to yourself. You’ll stay on sertraline for depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the regular floor today. Your vitals are stable, and labs keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hate the ICU noise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your insulin. You’ll now take 16 units of Lantus in the morning and 3 at dinner, plus sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Different from before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Endocrinology recommended this to give more consistent coverage. Your daughter was here for teaching—she’ll help you adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs are excellent. Glucose 98, bicarb 23, creatinine 0.6. Your body has fully recovered from the DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s amazing. I feel stronger too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning for discharge in a couple days. Home health will visit twice a day at first to help with insulin and checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about doing it alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You won’t be alone. Your daughter is involved, and the home nurses will be there. Plus, you’ll return to your outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your left wrist. You mentioned swelling. It shows mild soft tissue edema but no infection or fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been sore. I thought it might be infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of infection. It may be related to phlebitis from past IVs. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no treatment needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is clear, and ECG shows sinus tachycardia but no new changes. Heart is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t had any chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The small troponin rise was from stress, not a blockage. Keep taking your heart meds daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. We’ve restarted your blood pressure meds—amlodipine, lisinopril, metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed those before. I’ll try harder now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s hard. That’s why we’re building support around you. The goal is to prevent another hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check. You’re alert, labs are normal, and you walked to the bathroom fine. Discharge is approved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take all your meds, check your sugars, and call if you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my daughter will check on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Home health arrives tomorrow morning. They’ll help with insulin and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Diabetes clinic in one week. Psychiatry and primary care soon after. We’ll fax all records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final visit before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Take meds, check sugars, let someone know if I feel bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep working with your support team. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll try my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already started. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let the nurse know when you’re ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here because your blood sugar was very high when you came in. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I checked my blood sugar and it was over 500. I felt sick—nauseous, threw up once, and had a headache. I was worried I might be going into DKA again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good call. We checked your labs and your glucose was 505, but your bicarbonate was normal and no ketones, so it’s not DKA this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s a relief. But why is my sugar so high again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s because of a urinary tract infection. Your urine test showed a lot of white blood cells, and you had a low-grade fever. Infections make blood sugar harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel like I had a UTI. Just the nausea and headache. Is that common?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with diabetes. Sometimes infections don’t have the usual symptoms. We started you on an antibiotic in the ER—ceftriaxone—and we’ll continue treatment here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been taking my insulin like I’m supposed to. I didn’t skip any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you. Infections increase insulin resistance, so your usual dose isn’t enough. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re here to bring your sugars down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had this happen before. How long will I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably a few days. We want to make sure your infection clears and your sugars stabilize on the new insulin doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back—it’s E. coli, and it’s sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using. That’s great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the usual kind of bacteria for a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, E. coli is the most common cause. We’ll switch you to an oral antibiotic soon—Bactrim—for a few more days after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. I think I’m okay with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar this morning was 240, which is much better. We’re increasing your long-acting insulin from 25 to 30 units of Lantus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big jump. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and necessary. Your body needs more insulin right now because of the infection. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already. No more headache or nausea. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep you for a few more days to make sure your sugars stay under control and you’re responding to the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest blood sugar was 160, and you’re not spilling ketones. We’re also increasing your mealtime insulin—Humalog to 8 units for breakfast and lunch, 9 for dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll write that down. Should I keep these doses after I get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see. Once the infection clears, your insulin needs may go back down. If your sugars run low, go back to your old doses and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I don’t want to go low. That scares me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re safe. You’re doing well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober for a month now, thanks to naltrexone and therapy. I just want to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s really impressive. You’re on the right medications—sertraline and naltrexone—and we’ll keep those going. Your mood seems stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Depression used to make me want to drink. Now I’m learning other ways to cope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly the progress we want to see. Keep up with your outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray was clear, and your heart sounds are stable. We’re continuing your usual meds—lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that heart attack last year. I take the statin and aspirin every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Atorvastatin 80 mg helps prevent another one. Your numbers are stable, so no changes needed there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been checking my sugars every few hours. They’re mostly between 140 and 180 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent control. We’re confident we can discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I’m nervous about managing the new insulin doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a printed sheet with your new regimen. And remember—just go back to your old doses if sugars drop below 100.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your infection is responding, and your sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take Bactrim twice a day for three more days. You got the first half here, so just finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lantus 30 units in the morning, Humalog 8 with breakfast and lunch, 9 with dinner, plus sliding scale as needed. But if sugars run low, revert to your old doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I have follow-up with my endocrinologist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call your PCP if you have any concerns before then—especially if you develop fever, pain, or high sugars again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me get back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep up the good work with your sobriety and diabetes care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. This stay reminded me how important it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll see you in clinic, but hopefully not back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications. You should be out within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU because your blood sugar was extremely high and you were in diabetic ketoacidosis. Do you remember calling your kids to call an ambulance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I knew something was wrong. I hadn’t taken my fast-acting insulin for a few days. I was drinking a lot and just… didn’t care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your glucose was 830 when you arrived, and your body was producing ketones. We started an insulin drip and fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt so thirsty and my heart was racing. I knew it was DKA again. I’m sorry this keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not here to judge. We want to help you get better and prevent this from happening again. You also had very high potassium, which can be dangerous for the heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? I didn’t know that could happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in DKA, acidosis shifts potassium out of cells. Your EKG showed changes, so we gave calcium to protect your heart and are watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin was slightly elevated, likely from stress on the heart during DKA, not a heart attack. It’s improving now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My kidneys too—they said my creatinine was high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was 1.9, but it’s likely due to dehydration from DKA. We call that pre-renal azotemia. With fluids, it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much water. Just vodka.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on IV fluids and thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins because heavy drinking can deplete those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to cut down. I’m in an outpatient program, but I slipped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s honest. We’re not restarting naltrexone for now since you haven’t been taking it consistently. We’ll discuss that with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I do want help. I know my depression and drinking are messing with my diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We’ll make sure you have follow-up with your doctor and a mental health provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—239 this morning. The insulin drip is being adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better than 800. When will I be off the drip?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your acidosis resolves and you can eat, we’ll switch you to injections. Your anion gap is closing, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling less shaky. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a light diet. Also, your platelet count is low, which we’re watching. It could be from alcohol or liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now, but your PCP should check your liver function. We’re holding acetaminophen for now just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your creatinine is down to 0.9, and potassium is stable. We’re switching you to the floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on Lantus 28 units in the morning and Humalog 7 units before meals. A diabetes educator will review it with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s less Lantus than before. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your sugars are stabilizing. We’ll adjust based on your readings. Your A1c was 11%, so we know control has been tough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I need better support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. Social work will help connect you with resources, and you should talk to your doctor about counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking good. Glucose is 148, bicarbonate is 23. You’re almost ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. No more thirst or racing heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll make sure you have all your medications, including sertraline and your blood pressure pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking the sertraline. It helps, but I still drink when I’m down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The key is linking mental health and diabetes care. Your PCP can help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. Your vitals are stable, and labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your insulin, avoid alcohol, and follow up with your doctor within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll talk to them about counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We also gave you a vaginal cream for a yeast infection—use it for four nights.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know I had that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with high blood sugar. It should clear up now that your glucose is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other warnings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel short of breath, chest pain, or your blood sugar goes very high again, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t either. Take care of yourself. Your team is here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try my best. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over them with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your blood pressure is good now, so we restarted losartan and amlodipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take them every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep taking ferrous sulfate for your iron levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I sometimes forget, but I’ll set a reminder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. Small steps make a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to make changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I appreciate your patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly to finalize discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if you need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because your blood sugar was extremely high when you came in. You were confused and not feeling well. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I remember being really sick. Vomiting a lot. My sons called someone. I took some insulin but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your blood sugar was 1465—way too high. You were in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That happens when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy, which makes acids build up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I haven’t been taking my insulin regularly. I’ve been drinking a lot and not eating. I know I shouldn’t, but I’ve been stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The DKA also caused your kidneys to struggle, and your blood pressure was very low. We’ve started you on IV fluids and an insulin drip to correct this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay? I remember last time I was in, they said something about a small heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw a small rise in your heart enzyme, troponin. But it looks like it was due to the stress of DKA, not a blocked artery. We call it a Type 2 NSTEMI. We’re continuing your heart medications—like aspirin and metoprolol—to protect you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s a relief. What about my blood? I feel so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin was low—7.9, which means anemia. It’s likely from chronic blood loss, possibly in your stomach or intestines, especially with your history of alcohol use. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your levels kept dropping, so we gave you one unit of blood yesterday to help. Your hemoglobin is now stable at 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t even know. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also placed a central line in your neck to help deliver fluids and medications safely. Your labs showed very high potassium, which can be dangerous for the heart, so we treated that right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember my hands tingling. Was that from the potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a common symptom. We’ve corrected it with insulin and fluids. Your levels are much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your kidney function is improving—your creatinine is down from 2.9 to 1.1. That means the dehydration and DKA were stressing your kidneys, but they’re recovering with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been urinating more. But I still feel tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body has been through a lot. We also did an ultrasound of your kidneys—no blockages. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the anemia? Is it from my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. You’ve been on heavy alcohol use, which can cause ulcers or irritation. We’ve started you on pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and protect your lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend an endoscopy and colonoscopy after discharge to check for any sources of bleeding. Your primary doctor will help set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some changes on your chest X-ray. There’s a shadow in your right lung. It could be fluid, or possibly an infection. We’re not sure yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a dry cough. No fever, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. We don’t think it’s pneumonia, but we’re watching it. It might be related to fluid shifts from DKA. We’ll repeat the X-ray soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is much better—around 160. We’re transitioning you from the insulin drip to your regular shots: Lantus at night and Humalog with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take 28 units of Lantus. Why are we lowering it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your body is more sensitive to insulin now that you’re not in DKA. We’re starting at 22 units to avoid low blood sugar. We’ll adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I don’t want to crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your anemia is stable. Hemoglobin is 7.5. We’re discharging your home meds, including iron and folic acid, to help rebuild your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the naltrexone? I was taking that for alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing naltrexone. We also want you to reconnect with your therapist and AA sponsor. We’re setting you up with an intensive outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really want to stop drinking. It’s just hard when I’m stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. The program will help with both the drinking and the stress. Your mental health is just as important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the shadow is still there. But since you’re not having trouble breathing, we think it’s resolving slowly. No antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart ultrasound showed strong pumping function, but some high pressure in the lungs. It’s likely from the DKA stress. It should improve as you recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No damage to the heart muscle?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The wall motion is normal. Your heart is strong. We’ll keep you on your usual heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Blood sugar is steady, kidneys are normal, and you’re feeling more alert. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your insulin exactly as prescribed—22 units Lantus at night, 4 units Humalog with each meal, and use the sliding scale if your sugar is high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your blood pressure pills, aspirin, cholesterol medicine, sertraline, and naltrexone. And take the pantoprazole twice a day for your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try not to miss any. I know that’s what got me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all slip sometimes. The key is to get back on track quickly. Check your blood sugar four times a day and write it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final labs are excellent. Blood sugar 163, sodium and potassium normal, anion gap closed. Your body has fully corrected the DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Clearer in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your mental status has improved a lot since admission. You’re alert and oriented now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you tomorrow. You’ll go home with visiting nurse services to check on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve sent referrals: to your endocrinologist, primary care doctor, and gastroenterologist for the endoscopy. Your therapist will call you to set up rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make those appointments. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. If your blood sugar goes high or you start vomiting, come back right away. Don’t wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Your vitals are great—blood pressure 146/84, heart rate 85, oxygen 99% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: insulin every day, no alcohol, eat regularly, and keep your follow-up visits. You’ve got a strong support team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. I want to get healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we believe you can. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital now. You were brought in because your daughter found you very confused and not responding well. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I feel so weak. My stomach hurt so bad, and I was throwing up. I stopped taking my insulin because I wasn’t eating…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood sugar was extremely high when you arrived, and your body was in a state called diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That happens when there’s not enough insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: DKA again? I’ve had that before… Is that why I felt so out of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Without insulin, your body starts breaking down fat for energy, which creates acids. That, plus dehydration, made you very sick. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had a cough and stopped drinking alcohol cold turkey last week. I thought maybe that was making me feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could have contributed. Stopping alcohol suddenly can affect your appetite and how you manage your diabetes. We’ll keep an eye on that, but right now, the main issue is getting your sugars and chemistry balanced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My hands feel tingly… and I’m still so cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were hypothermic when you arrived—your temperature was low. We’re warming you up slowly. The tingling could be from electrolyte imbalances. We’re correcting those carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared… Is my heart okay? I remember last time I was in, I had a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have a history of heart problems, and your EKG and labs show strain, but no active heart attack this time. Your heart is under stress from the DKA, but we’re monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a central line in your neck to help deliver fluids and medications more effectively. It’s working well, and a chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that… it was uncomfortable. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common procedure. The X-ray showed no complications like a collapsed lung. We’ll keep it clean and remove it when you no longer need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidneys aren’t filtering well right now—acute kidney injury. It’s likely due to dehydration from vomiting and high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in most cases like this, kidney function improves once we correct the dehydration and DKA. We’re watching your urine output and labs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic before… my last admission, I needed a transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low again—8.0, which is concerning. We’re checking for sources of bleeding, but it may be chronic, related to your history of GI blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I get another transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off for now. Your vital signs are stable, and we want to see if your levels improve with hydration and treatment. We’ll recheck in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was very high earlier—6.5—which can affect your heart. We gave you treatments to bring it down, and it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my heart felt funny?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. High potassium can cause irregular heartbeats. We’re monitoring your EKG and will keep checking your levels daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection in your bloodstream. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my lungs? I’ve been coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid buildup in the lungs—pulmonary edema. It’s likely from heart strain and fluid shifts during DKA, not pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your white count is elevated, but that can happen with DKA alone. No signs of bacterial infection, so we’re holding off on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental status is improving. You’re more alert today—that’s a good sign your treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little clearer. My stomach still hurts, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal pain is likely from the DKA. As your acid levels normalize, it should get better. We’ll keep your pain managed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your anion gap is closing—down from 41 to 18. That means the ketoacidosis is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’re starting to transition you from IV insulin to subcutaneous injections, like you take at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll take them this time… I just felt so sick last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Illness and stress make diabetes harder to manage. We’ll work with you on a plan to prevent this from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the fluid in your lungs is improving. We’re also seeing better kidney function—your creatinine is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about my heart and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, but you’re moving in the right direction. Your platelet count was low earlier, but it’s starting to rise, so that’s improving as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need close follow-up with your endocrinologist. We’ll also refer you back to the outpatient alcohol rehab program—you were doing well before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need help with that. Stopping on my own was a mistake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not easy. We’ll restart naltrexone to help with cravings, and pantoprazole for stomach protection. All your usual meds, including insulin, will be sent to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll remove the central line before you leave. You’re stable to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll take better care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call your doctor if your sugars go high or you feel unwell. Keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your stool test was negative for C. difficile, and your MRSA screen was clear. No infections detected during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about picking something up in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We take precautions to prevent that. You’ve done really well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge paperwork. You’ll be leaving soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just want to get home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. And remember, if anything changes—like vomiting, confusion, or high sugars—go to the ER or call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re rooting for you. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your daughter is here. We’ll get you discharged in the next hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re officially discharged. Here’s your medication list and follow-up instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Thank you.
